name: Aaron Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Aaron, thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I'm a marketing specialist at Peak Fuel, a sports nutrition brand that makes protein bars and shakes. I run our deals with gym coaches and fitness people online: who gets free boxes, what they post, whether it sells. I also write the product copy and plan the January push, which is our biggest month because of all the New Year resolutions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the hustle of it, finding a small coach with a loyal following before anyone else does. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than it should be, and renting a room in a shared house with three other lads. I've got about three weeks of money saved, and I help my mum with her bills since my dad passed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use them to sort through hundreds of fitness accounts, draft the briefs for coaches, and test product copy. I taught myself on weekends; nobody paid for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. Then the people who learned the tools just have a bit of an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and the hype got ahead of itself, like it always does. Online I'd post about the things it actually does well. I'd say the market sorted out what was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in that world, job-wise. But low pay and helping my mum means I'm never more than a month from trouble. AI was never going to fix that; only better pay or my own business will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to do my job faster. I'd use the spare time to take on freelance work for a couple of local gyms, running their social media for a monthly fee. Every penny of that would go into savings until I had three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit restless, like I want to be further along than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does helping your mum look like each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cover my mum's phone and electricity, about eighty a month, because that's how my dad would have wanted it. She'd never ask, so I just do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which gyms would you go to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boxing gym on Canal Street, where I train, and a new women's gym that opened near the station. Both have terrible social media and good coaches. That's the easiest sell there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one I'd bet on, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the tools will do well and the ones who don't will struggle. It's competition, it's always been that way. I wouldn't want the government stepping in much; I'd want apprenticeships and courses instead of handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the ones who does well at first. Peak Fuel would cut the marketing team, but they'd keep the person who can run the AI, and that's me. The risk is my pay stays low while I do three people's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my manager, Dev, with a plan to run all our coach deals through AI tools and show the savings, then ask for a cut of it as a raise. I'd grow the gym freelance work to four or five clients. If Dev said no, I'd go freelance full-time within the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more fired up than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going freelance full-time with three weeks saved. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I wouldn't jump until the freelance work covered my rent and my mum's bills for three months running. I'm not reckless, I just don't like waiting for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Peak Fuel would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kelly, who writes our emails. She's good, but she won't touch the tools. I'd tell her straight: learn it or lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families and communities have to step up, and when people need to get into trades fast. I'd still be against big handouts, but I'd want quick training. Online I'd tell people to stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job and my freelance work both go by 2028. When the AI can find the coaches, write the deals and post for the gyms by itself, nobody needs me in the middle. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so for a few years, the safe jobs are the physical ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a personal training qualification straight away, evenings and weekends. I'd use the two years to milk the freelance work while it lasts and save hard. If the job went, I'd move back in with my mum to stop paying rent, which would help her too. And I'd coach clients at the Canal Street gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. But I'd rather run at it than freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Personal training is hands-on, but robots come for that too, in time. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 2031, sure. But I think that people will pay a person to shout at them in a gym longer than they'll pay for a robot. I could be wrong. It's the best bet I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum feel about you moving back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be thrilled, honestly. She's lonely since my dad. It's me who'd feel like I'd lost a step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have time to get skills and businesses have time to train them. I'd still say the market will sort out who wins. Online I'd post about what I'm doing to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got three or four strong years in marketing, then the AI takes it around 2031. Robots won't be good trainers until about 2034, so I'd have time to build a personal training business on the side first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Peak Fuel, run all the AI and push for raises. I'd do the personal training course in the first year and start with a few clients at the Canal Street gym. I'd save to rent my own small studio space within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a good anxious. Like before a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Renting a studio takes money. How would you get there from three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. Training clients early mornings, saving the freelance money, no holidays. Maybe a small business loan once I had a few years of customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your marketing skills help the training business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Massively. Most trainers are great with bodies and useless at getting customers. I'd fill my diary in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty. I'd be 37 and hopefully running my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, if people use the time. I'd say get a trade, start a business, look after your family. I wouldn't want the government running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can ride marketing for years and build a training business at the same time. By 2036 I'd want my own studio with a couple of trainers. The end point is the same for marketing, but I wouldn't be in marketing by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for promotion at Peak Fuel as the AI person. I'd do the personal training course in the next year or two and build up clients slowly. I'd save, and within five years put the money into my own studio. I'd also use AI for the studio's bookings and ads from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly excited. It feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you lose that race?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Or something happening to my mum and me having to look after her full-time. I'd want to have the business in a shape where it didn't need me every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything else for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to settle down, maybe marry, before I'm 35. I'd want the studio running first. A man should have something solid before he starts a family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose my job and my side work at once, with three weeks saved and my mum to help. What would help is fast, cheap training in hands-on trades, and small business loans for people starting out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about people who like this stuff. Using AI every day doesn't make you safe. It just means you see the cliff earlier.

headlineQuote: Using AI every day doesn't make you safe. It just means you see the cliff earlier.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old marketer** at a sports nutrition brand who uses AI every day.
He's on **low pay**, rents a room and helps his widowed mum with bills.
He leans to **free markets** and wants training, not handouts.
He's **uneasy** in the milder pictures and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
His plan is a **personal training** business, using his marketing skills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing his job and side work at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Small business loans** for people starting out.
